rationale: The student confuses a small, interesting descriptive detail ('bees are yellow') with the central idea ('bees help plants'). A direct side-by-side comparison makes the conceptual difference between the overarching 'big idea' and a supporting 'small detail' visually and structurally distinct.
intent: Present a side-by-side comparison of 'Main Idea' (the big umbrella topic covering the whole text) versus 'Detail' (one small fact or sentence that supports the big idea). Use a simple Grade 2 friendly example (such as dogs having jobs vs. dogs having fur) completely separate from bees or pollination so the original passage answer is not spoiled.

data.title: Main Idea vs. Supporting Detail
data.intro: When we read a story or a book, it is like looking at a big umbrella house. Let us learn how to find the big main idea and the small details that help hold it up!

item1.name: The Main Idea
item1.description: The big umbrella thought that tells us what the whole story is mostly about.
item1.visualPrompt: A giant green umbrella covering all the other smaller pictures below it.
points: It tells what the whole story is about.
It is the most important point.
It covers everything in the text like a big umbrella.

item2.name: A Supporting Detail
item2.description: One small fact or piece of information that helps prove or explain the big idea.
item2.visualPrompt: A single raindrops or small puzzle piece pointing up to the big umbrella.
points: It is just one small piece of the story.
It gives an extra fact or color.
It helps prove why the main idea is true.

synthesis.mainInsight: The main idea is the big roof of the house, and details are the little bricks that help build it.
keyDifferences: The main idea is about the whole text, but a detail is only about one small part.
The main idea is the most important point, while details just give extra facts.
keySimilarities: Both are found inside the same story or book.
Both work together to help us understand what we are reading.
synthesis.commonMisconception: Thinking that every cool or fun fact in a story is the main idea.

whenToUse.item1Context: Use the main idea when someone asks you, 'What was this story mostly about?'
whenToUse.item2Context: Use details when someone asks you to prove your answer with a fact from the text.

gates.question: The main idea tells us what the whole story is mostly about, while a supporting detail is just one small fact.
gates.rationale: Great job! The main idea is the big umbrella for the whole text, and a detail is just one small piece that supports it.

gates.question: A supporting detail covers the whole story just like the main idea does.
gates.rationale: Not quite! A supporting detail is only one small part of the story, whereas the main idea covers the whole thing.

judgement.reasoning: The detour directly addresses the student's exact misconception (confusing an interesting fact/detail with the main idea) by framing Main Idea vs. Supporting Detail side by side using accessible metaphors (umbrella/house bricks). It strips away complex text to focus on the prerequisite concept definition, does not leak the bees passage, and uses simple check questions appropriate for Grade 2.
judgement.verdict: A teacher would readily use this side-by-side comparison to clarify the difference between an umbrella topic and a small supporting detail before sending the student back to the passage.
